name: Jamal Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm the farming and rural business reporter for the Westmoor Herald, a regional news site with a print edition on Fridays. Mornings I go through livestock market prices, grain futures and planning notices, then I'm out in the car to a farm, an auction mart or a feed company. I also record a weekly farming podcast in a cupboard we call the studio.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Standing in a farmyard with someone who's been up since four, hearing how a decision in a capital city lands on their milk cheque. My parents run a dairy farm in the next valley, so I know what it costs. Farmers can smell a reporter who doesn't, and they won't talk to them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every single day. It summarises the market reports, transcribes my interviews in the car, and drafts the price round-up that I then check. That frees me two or three hours a week, which I spend out on farms. I'm a big believer in using whatever tool makes you better at the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said all along, it's a good tool and nothing more. I'd probably post that the reporters who learned it got a head start and kept it. I'm not shy about that online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it suits me fine. I'm already using it more than anyone at the Herald, so I keep my edge and the job doesn't change underneath me. My savings are solid and there are plenty of comms jobs with farm bodies and food firms if the Herald ever struggled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I'd finally launch the paid newsletter for farmers that I've been planning, a weekly guide to prices and policy for about five dollars a month. I'd use AI to do the number crunching and spend my own time on the phone calls with farmers. If it got to a few hundred subscribers, I'd think about going part-time at the Herald.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, actually, because I'd want to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about money or the job that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've got over a year of costs saved, and a small stake in the family farm. The Herald is losing print readers, but that's been true my whole career, and I've never relied on print.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the Herald mind you building your own newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my editor first and keep it to farm markets, which the Herald doesn't cover in depth. I believe in doing things straight. If they said no, I'd respect that and wait a bit.

say: I'd say AI is **a good tool** and nothing more.
I'd post that reporters who learned it got **a head start**.
think: I think a plateau suits me, since I **keep my edge** at the Herald.
With **solid savings** and plenty of comms jobs, I'm not worried.
do: Launch a **paid newsletter** on farm prices and policy at five dollars a month.
Ask my editor's **permission first** and keep it to farm markets.
Consider going **part-time** if it reaches a few hundred subscribers.
feel: I'd feel **calm**, and a bit **restless** to build something of my own.
S0.quote: I'd use AI to do the number crunching and spend my own time on the phone calls with farmers.
fieldNote: Jamal sees AI as **his advantage** and wants to turn it into a business of his own.
His **family farm stake** and a year of savings make him unusually relaxed.
He combines **enterprise** with loyalty, asking his editor before starting anything.

steps.text: Keep using AI daily for market reports and interview transcripts
Launch a five-dollar weekly farm prices newsletter with the editor's blessing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small, focused outlets to compete with big ones. I'd probably write a column saying the market will reward reporters who add something a machine can't. I'd be upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I come out ahead. The price round-ups and press release rewrites at the Herald go to software, and some colleagues lose hours or jobs, but I've already moved my own time to farm visits. The risk is the Herald deciding one rural reporter is too many, and if that happens I'd already have the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the whole price round-up so it runs itself, and offer to set it up for the Herald too. I'd grow the newsletter, add a paid audio version of the podcast, and aim for a thousand subscribers by the end of the first year. I'd also put some savings into a share of a cattle-scanning startup a friend from college runs, because farm tech will grow in this world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a little excited. I know that sounds hard on the people who'll struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our news editor, Sandra, who's in her fifties and still prints everything out to read it. Sandra's brilliant at spotting a story, but she'd hate learning a new system. I'd offer to sit with her, but I can't make her want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some would say government should help the people pushed out. What do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd rather see apprenticeships and retraining paid partly by the firms that save the money. I don't think a cheque in the post fixes much, because people want work, not handouts.

say: I'd say **small, focused outlets** can now compete with big ones.
I'd write that **the market** will reward reporters who add something a machine can't.
think: I think **I come out ahead**, because I've already moved my time to farm visits.
If the Herald cuts **one rural reporter**, I'd already have the newsletter.
do: Automate the **price round-up** fully and offer it to the Herald.
Grow the newsletter to **a thousand subscribers** with a paid podcast.
Invest savings in a friend's **cattle-scanning startup**.
feel: I'd feel **calm** and a little **excited**, though I know others will struggle.
S1.quote: I don't think a cheque in the post fixes much, because people want work, not handouts.
fieldNote: Jamal expects to **gain** and builds a backup before the Herald could cut him.
His free-market view shows in his **policy answer**: retraining paid by firms, not cheques.
He'd help an older editor but accepts he **can't force** her to change.

steps.text: Set the price round-up to run automatically for the Herald
Grow the farm newsletter to a thousand paying subscribers
Buy a stake in a college friend's cattle-scanning startup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's be practical. Farmers have lived through foot-and-mouth and price crashes, and they'll get through this too. I'd keep my public line steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too short for my plans. If AI can write a better market newsletter than me for pennies, my subscribers go too, not just my Herald job. What's left is the trust farmers have in me and the farm itself, because the robots for milking and fencing don't arrive until about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the Herald job as long as it lasts and pour my time into the newsletter while people still pay for a name they know. I'd talk to my parents about coming back to the farm part-time, learning the business side properly, because a dairy farm needs hands and a head for at least those three extra years. I'd keep my savings liquid rather than locking them into anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which isn't like me. I'm used to being early, and this would be too fast to be early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your parents take that conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad would say he always knew I'd come home. Mum would worry I was giving up. I'd tell them both I'm not giving up on anything, I'm just choosing the part of farming that machines reach last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said keep savings liquid. Why not invest in the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if robot milkers get cheap in 2031, the value of what we buy now could fall. I'd rather have cash and see what's worth buying when it lands.

say: I'd say **let's be practical**, because farmers have survived crashes before.
I'd keep my **public line steady** and not panic online.
think: I think two years is **too short** for my newsletter plans.
AI could write a market newsletter **for pennies**, taking my subscribers too.
The farm has **about three years** before robots reach milking and fencing.
do: Keep the Herald job and push the **newsletter** while names still sell.
Return to the **family farm** part-time to learn the business side.
Keep savings **in cash** rather than locking them up.
feel: I'd feel **anxious**, which isn't like me, because this is **too fast**.
S2.quote: I'm not giving up on anything, I'm just choosing the part of farming that machines reach last.
fieldNote: Jamal's usual edge, **being early**, stops working when AGI comes in two years.
He turns to the **family dairy farm**, using the three-year robot gap.
He thinks carefully about **asset values**, holding cash until robot costs are clear.

steps.text: Work part-time on my parents' dairy farm learning the business side
Push the farm newsletter hard while readers still pay for a name
Keep over a year of savings in cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty of time if you start now. I'd probably host a podcast episode with farmers on what it means for them. Publicly I'd be encouraging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see the reporting side ending around 2031, and the newsletter with it. But five years lets me build the farm side properly. By the time robots arrive on farms around 2034, I'd want to be the person in our valley who knows how to buy and run them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both jobs going for three years and save hard. I'd do a part-time course in farm business management at the agricultural college. In year three or four, I'd start working with my parents on a plan to bring in robot milkers when the price is right, so the farm is ready rather than surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a busy way. It's a lot to fit in, but it's a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about your parents' generation on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Dad's 61 and doesn't trust anything with a screen. I'd want to be the one who makes the change gently, so he doesn't feel replaced on his own land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd give up in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the idea of journalism as my life's work. I'd miss it. But I'd rather leave journalism on my own terms than be shown the door in 2031.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty of time** if you start now.
I'd host a **podcast episode** with farmers on what it means.
think: I think the **reporting side** and the newsletter both end around 2031.
I want to be the one in our valley who can **run farm robots** by 2034.
do: Keep **both jobs** for three years and save hard.
Take a part-time **farm business course** at the agricultural college.
Plan **robot milkers** for the family farm with my parents by year four.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy** but busy, because I'd **have a plan**.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave journalism on my own terms than be shown the door in 2031.
fieldNote: Jamal treats the extra time as a chance to **prepare the farm** for robots.
He wants to change things **gently** so his father doesn't feel replaced.
He admits he'd **miss journalism**, which he rarely shows.

steps.text: Take a part-time farm business management course at the agricultural college
Save hard from both the Herald and the newsletter for three years
Plan with my parents to buy robot milkers when prices fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real gift and anyone who doesn't use it only has themselves to blame. I'd say that on the podcast, probably more bluntly than I should. I believe people can do a lot with a decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I'd have ten years of reporting, a decade-old newsletter with loyal readers, and time to take over the farm side as Dad steps back. By 2036 I'd be 37 with savings and land, which is a strong place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep reporting and keep using every new AI tool as it comes, because they'd make me faster each year. I'd grow the newsletter slowly and put profits into the farm, maybe new sheds and better herd records. I'd plan to step into running the farm properly around 2033.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. It feels like enough time to do it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the people who wait. Some of my friends from college think it'll never happen. I'd tell them, but I can't make them listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people have themselves to blame. Is that fair to everyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not to everyone. Someone with no savings or with kids has less room than me, so I'd be gentler with them. I'd still say ten years is long enough to try something.

say: I'd say ten years is **a real gift** for anyone who uses it.
I'd say it **bluntly** on the podcast, maybe more than I should.
think: I think **I'd do well**, with ten years to build the newsletter and farm.
At 37 I'd have **savings and land**, which is a strong place to be.
do: Keep reporting and adopt **every new AI tool** as it arrives.
Put newsletter profits into **sheds and herd records** on the farm.
Plan to **take over the farm** around 2033.
feel: I'd feel **calm**, because ten years is **enough time** to do it right.
S4.quote: Someone with no savings or with kids has less room than me, so I'd be gentler with them.
fieldNote: Jamal feels **secure** with ten years, thanks to savings, land and adaptability.
His **blunt view** that people have themselves to blame softened when challenged.
His long-term plan is **the family farm**, funded by the newsletter.

steps.text: Adopt each new AI tool at the Herald as it arrives
Put newsletter profits into new sheds and herd records
Take over running the family dairy farm around 2033

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. It's too fast even for someone like me who likes change, and it would wipe out the newsletter before it had a chance. What would help is apprenticeships and retraining funded by the firms making the savings, and less red tape for small farms that want to bring in new machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what it does to trust. Farmers trust me because I've stood in their yards, and if every story is written by a machine, I don't know who they'll believe. That worries me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: Farmers trust me because I've stood in their yards, and if every story is written by a machine, I don't know who they'll believe.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old farming reporter** at a regional news site, from a dairy farming family.
He's **traditional, free-market and adaptive**, using AI every day and planning a paid newsletter.
In the milder pictures he expects to **come out ahead** and builds his own business.
With **AGI by 2028** he's anxious and turns to the family farm's three-year robot gap.
With ten years he feels calm, planning to **run the farm** with savings and land.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which is too fast even for him and would sink the newsletter.
whatWouldHelp: **Retraining** paid by firms that save money, and less **red tape** for small farms buying machines.
